tips.title: Two acts up, three acts down
tips.body: Crowned by the end of Act 2; Banquo and the ghost in Act 3; the apparitions and the Macduffs in Act 4; the sleepwalking, the wood and Macduff in Act 5. Place any extract by where it sits on that curve.

tips.title: The murder is off stage
tips.body: The audience never sees Duncan die. It sees the dagger before and hears the voice after, so the murder is lived through Macbeth's mind. A structural point worth a sentence in any Act 2 answer.

tips.title: Echoes are the whole-text move
tips.body: Water and perfume; murdered sleep and sleepwalking; Macdonwald's head and Macbeth's. Pair a line in the extract with its echo and you have a structural point and the second bullet at once.

tips.title: The prophecies in order
tips.body: King hereafter; beware Macduff; none of woman born; Birnam Wood to Dunsinane. Each is true in word, and each misleads him.

tips.title: Who dies where
tips.body: Duncan, Act 2, off stage; Banquo, Act 3, Fleance escapes; the Macduffs, Act 4; Lady Macbeth, Act 5, off stage; Macbeth, killed by Macduff.

why.matters: The extract question prints one scene and asks about the whole play, so the order of the play has to be yours. Knowing it is not enough, though: Shakespeare built this tragedy with a rise that is over in two acts, a fall that takes three, and echoes that make the end answer the beginning. Each choice does something to an audience that a plot summary cannot. Twelve of the thirty marks are for methods, and structure is one. A student who knows the story can retell it; a student who knows the build can place any extract and say what its place does.

examples.title: The rise-and-fall story you already know
examples.body: Films about a gangster's career follow the shape of *Macbeth*: a quick climb to the top in the first half, then a long slide as each crime needs another to cover it, and a death that the opening scenes made inevitable. The shape tells the audience what the story is about before any character says it: not getting power, but what keeping it costs.

examples.title: An ending that answers the opening
examples.body: Novels and films often end on an image that repeats their first one, changed: the same house, the same road, the same line spoken by a different person. *Macbeth* does it with a head on the battlements and a head held up by Macduff. The repetition is how a story shows, without explaining, how far it has travelled.

steps.title: A soldier, three witches and a promise
steps.body:
*Macbeth* is Shakespeare's shortest tragedy, and it moves fast. Scotland is at war. Macbeth, Thane of Glamis, is a general in the army of King Duncan, and he has just won a battle against a rebel, Macdonwald, and an invading Norwegian army.

**Before we meet him, we hear of him.** A wounded soldier tells Duncan how Macbeth fought: “Till he unseam’d him from the nave to the chops”, “And fix’d his head upon our battlements”. The soldier calls him “For brave Macbeth”, and Duncan gives him the title of a traitor just condemned, the Thane of Cawdor.

**Before we hear of him, the witches.** The play opens on three witches in thunder and lightning, agreeing to meet Macbeth, and chanting “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” (the witches, 1.1). His first words, walking off the battlefield, echo them without his knowing: “So foul and fair a day I have not seen” (Macbeth, 1.3).

**The promise.** On the heath the witches hail him as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and king hereafter. Minutes later, messengers tell him he is Thane of Cawdor. One prophecy has come true, and the question the whole play asks has been planted: will he wait for the third, or make it happen?

boxes.title: Duncan
boxes.body: King of Scotland, old and trusting

boxes.title: Macbeth
boxes.body: Thane of Glamis, the victorious general

boxes.title: Banquo
boxes.body: His fellow general, promised kings for sons

boxes.title: The witches
boxes.body: Three weird sisters who hail Macbeth king

visuals.alt: Four boxes on who matters at the start of Macbeth: Duncan, Macbeth, Banquo and the witches, each with a line on who they are

check.prompt: What title does Duncan give Macbeth after the battle, and whose was it?
check.solution: Thane of Cawdor. The old Thane of Cawdor had sided with Norway and is executed; his title goes to the man who beat him. Macbeth was already Thane of Glamis, so the second of the witches' three greetings comes true as soon as it is spoken, and the audience watches him start to wonder about the third.

markScheme.description: Thane of Cawdor, the title of a traitor who had just been condemned to death

options: Prince of Cumberland, the title of the king's heir
Thane of Cawdor, the title of a traitor who had just been condemned to death
Thane of Fife, the title that belonged to Macduff
Thane of Glamis, a new title that Duncan created for him as a reward for the victory over the Norwegian army

steps.title: Acts 1 and 2: from the heath to the murder
steps.body:
**Act 1.** Duncan names his son Malcolm as his heir, Prince of Cumberland, and Macbeth sees the obstacle at once: “That is a step On which I must fall down, or else o’erleap”. “Stars, hide your fires” (Macbeth, 1.4). He writes to his wife. Lady Macbeth reads the letter, fears his nature is “too full o’ th’ milk of human kindness”, and calls on spirits to “unsex me here”. Duncan arrives at their castle at Inverness as a guest. Alone, Macbeth talks himself out of the murder and tells his wife “We will proceed no further in this business”; in one conversation she talks him back into it.

**Act 2.** At night Macbeth sees a dagger that is not there, “Is this a dagger which I see before me” (Macbeth, 2.1), and goes to Duncan's chamber. The murder happens off stage. He comes back with the bloody daggers still in his hands; his wife takes them back and smears the sleeping grooms with blood. There is knocking at the gate. In the morning Macduff finds the body, Macbeth kills the grooms before they can speak, and Duncan's sons flee, Malcolm to England and Donalbain to Ireland, which makes them look guilty. Macbeth is crowned.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of Acts 1 and 2: the witches hail Macbeth, the Cawdor prophecy comes true, Malcolm is named heir, Lady Macbeth persuades Macbeth, Duncan is murdered off stage, and Macbeth is crowned

check.prompt: Put these five moments from Acts 1 and 2 in the order the play presents them.
check.solution: The prophecy, then the obstacle, then the refusal and the persuasion, then the dagger on the way to the chamber, then the discovery in the morning. The refusal matters most: Macbeth decides against the murder before he does it, so the play makes the persuasion the hinge of Act 1.

markScheme.description: the five moments in order

items: The witches hail Macbeth as king hereafter
Duncan names Malcolm Prince of Cumberland
Macbeth tells his wife they will proceed no further
Macbeth sees a dagger before him
Macduff discovers the body of Duncan

steps.title: Act 3: Banquo, the banquet, the ghost
steps.body:
The crown does not bring peace. The witches promised Banquo that his descendants would be kings, and Macbeth broods on it: “Upon my head they plac’d a fruitless crown” (Macbeth, 3.1). Banquo suspects him: “Thou hast it now, King, Cawdor, Glamis, all” (Banquo, 3.1).

**Banquo.** Macbeth hires murderers to kill Banquo and his son Fleance on their way back to the palace. He does not tell his wife: “Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck” (Macbeth, 3.2). Banquo is killed; his last words are “Fly, good Fleance, fly”, and Fleance escapes.

**The banquet.** That night Macbeth hosts a feast for the lords of Scotland. Banquo's ghost enters and sits in Macbeth's place, and only Macbeth can see it: “Never shake Thy gory locks at me” (Macbeth, 3.4). Lady Macbeth covers for him and sends the guests away. Alone with her he decides to go back to the witches, and sees how far he has gone: “I am in blood Stepp’d in so far” (Macbeth, 3.4).

rows: The lords see him lose control
He is too deep in blood to turn
props.title: Act 3 in three moments

visuals.alt: A table of three moments in Act 3: the murder of Banquo, the banquet and the ghost, and the decision to return to the witches, with what each costs Macbeth

check.prompt: Why does the escape of Fleance matter to the structure of the play?
check.solution: Macbeth kills Banquo to stop the witches' promise of kings from Banquo's line. With Fleance alive, the promise survives and the murder has bought nothing. From this point Macbeth's crimes stop working: he kills more and controls less. Fleance does not return to fight; it is Macduff who kills Macbeth.

markScheme.description: It means the witches' promise to Banquo can still come true, so Macbeth's second murder fails in its purpose

options: It has no effect; Fleance does not appear again and the play forgets him
It means Fleance can return in Act 5 to kill Macbeth in single combat and take the crown that the witches promised his father
It means the witches' promise to Banquo can still come true, so Macbeth's second murder fails in its purpose
It shows that the murderers were paid too little

steps.title: Acts 4 and 5: the apparitions, Macduff, the fall
steps.body:
**Act 4.** Macbeth goes to the witches, who show him three apparitions. The first warns “Beware Macduff; Beware the Thane of Fife” (an apparition, 4.1). The second promises that “none of woman born Shall harm Macbeth”. The third says he will not be beaten until “Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill” comes against him. Then a line of eight kings, Banquo's descendants. Told that Macduff has fled to England, Macbeth has Macduff's wife and children murdered. In England Macduff hears the news: “All my pretty ones” (Macduff, 4.3). He and Malcolm raise an army.

**Act 5.** Lady Macbeth walks in her sleep, washing her hands, “Out, damned spot” (Lady Macbeth, 5.1), watched by a doctor and a gentlewoman. Malcolm's soldiers cut branches from Birnam Wood to hide their numbers, so the wood moves. Lady Macbeth dies, by her own hand as it is thought; Macbeth hears of it and says “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow” (Macbeth, 5.5). Facing Macduff, he learns that Macduff was “from his mother’s womb Untimely ripp’d” (Macduff, 5.8): born by caesarean, and so not of woman born. He fights on and is killed. Macduff enters with his head, and Malcolm is hailed king.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of Acts 4 and 5: three apparitions, the murder of Macduff's family, Malcolm and Macduff raise an army, Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and dies, Birnam Wood moves, and Macduff kills Macbeth

check.prompt: How does the prophecy that none of woman born shall harm Macbeth come true without being false?
check.solution: The words were true and the meaning was a trap. Macbeth heard that no man could kill him; the prophecy said only that no one born of woman in the usual way could. Macduff's birth by caesarean fits the words exactly. The witches never lie in the play: they tell truths that mislead, which is what Banquo warned of in Act 1.

markScheme.description: Macduff was delivered by caesarean, untimely ripped from his mother, so in the prophecy's own words he was not of woman born

options: Macbeth kills himself, so no one else harms him
The witches were lying, and Macbeth realises it only after the battle is over and he has been defeated by the English army under Siward
Malcolm kills Macbeth, and Malcolm was born abroad
Macduff was delivered by caesarean, untimely ripped from his mother, so in the prophecy's own words he was not of woman born

steps.title: The shape of a tragedy: rise and fall
steps.body: A Shakespearean tragedy follows a great man from a height to his death, and the fall comes from something in him as well as from the world. *Macbeth* has the clearest shape of any of them: a rise that is over by Act 2 and a fall that takes the rest of the play.

visuals.problem: Set out the rise and fall of Macbeth act by act, and say where the turning point comes.

steps.text: Act 1: praised, promised, tempted. The bravest man in Scotland is hailed king and talks himself out of murder, then is talked back in.
steps.note: The height, and the flaw showing: ambition, with a conscience still resisting it.

steps.text: Act 2: the murder and the crown. The crime succeeds; the sons flee; he is king.
steps.note: The top of the rise, reached in the first third of the play.

steps.text: Act 3: Banquo killed, Fleance escaped, the ghost at the feast. The second crime fails and he loses control in public.
steps.note: The turning point: from here the crimes stop working.

steps.text: Act 4: the apparitions, and the murder of a family who threaten nothing.
steps.note: The lowest moral point: violence with no purpose but fear.

steps.text: Act 5: his wife dead, the wood moving, the man not of woman born. He dies fighting.
steps.note: The fall completed, and a last flash of the soldier of Act 1.

visuals.alt: A table of Macbeth's rise and fall in five acts: praised and tempted, murders and is crowned, loses control, kills without purpose, falls and dies fighting

check.prompt: Why do many readers place the turning point in Act 3 rather than at the murder of Duncan?
check.solution: The murder of Duncan is the top of the rise: it works, and he is crowned. Act 3 is where things turn: the second murder fails because Fleance escapes, and the ghost at the banquet shows the lords that something is wrong with their king. Lady Macbeth dies in Act 5, and he is crowned at the end of Act 2.

markScheme.description: Act 3 is where his crimes stop succeeding: Fleance escapes, and the ghost breaks his control in public

options: Act 3 is where his crimes stop succeeding: Fleance escapes, and the ghost breaks his control in public
Because the murder of Duncan happens off stage, so it cannot count as a turning point in the structure of the play at all
Because Macbeth is not yet king until Act 3
Because Lady Macbeth dies in Act 3

steps.title: Echoes: how the end answers the beginning
steps.body:
Shakespeare builds *Macbeth* out of echoes, so that the end of the play answers its beginning, and a student who knows the pairs can write about structure with precision.

**Two traitors, two heads.** In Act 1 Macbeth kills the rebel Macdonwald and “And fix’d his head upon our battlements”; the traitor Thane of Cawdor is executed, and of his death Malcolm says “Nothing in his life Became him like the leaving it” (Malcolm, 1.4). In Act 5 Macbeth is the traitor, and Macduff enters with his head: “Behold, where stands Th’ usurper’s cursed head” (Macduff, 5.8). The play begins and ends with a traitor killed and a head displayed.

**Water and blood.** After the murder Lady Macbeth says “A little water clears us of this deed” (Lady Macbeth, 2.2). Walking in her sleep in Act 5 she says “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand” (Lady Macbeth, 5.1). The line of Act 2 is answered by the line of Act 5.

**Sleep.** After the murder Macbeth hears a voice cry that he has murdered sleep: “Macbeth does murder sleep” (Macbeth, 2.2). In Act 5 his wife cannot sleep, and walks.

**The witches' words.** They open the play with a riddle about foul and fair, and their last prophecies are riddles too; Macbeth's first words echo them, and his last hope rests on them.

rows: Macbeth's head held up by Macduff
Lady Macbeth walks in her sleep
Fair is foul, and foul is fair
None of woman born; Birnam Wood
props.title: Four echoes

visuals.alt: A table of four echoes in Macbeth, each pairing an early moment with the late moment that answers it: heads, water, sleep and the witches' riddles

check.prompt: What does the echo between A little water clears us of this deed and All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand show?
check.solution: In Act 2 she dismisses the blood as something water can wash off; in Act 5 she cannot get rid of it, and the smell of it is on her hand in her sleep. The echo measures her collapse in her own words. Naming both lines and the distance between them is a structural point about character.

markScheme.description: The confidence of Act 2 has become the guilt of Act 5: a stain that will not wash out

options: That the murder was committed with perfume rather than a dagger
The confidence of Act 2 has become the guilt of Act 5: a stain that will not wash out
That Lady Macbeth was never guilty
That Lady Macbeth has grown fond of perfume since she became queen and uses it to cover the smell of the castle

steps.title: Which act, and who is there?
steps.body:
The paper is closed book, and the extract question asks you to move from the printed scene to the play as a whole. That move is only possible if the order of the play is yours. Try these from memory first.

1. In which act is Duncan murdered, and does the audience see it?
2. Who escapes when Banquo is killed, and why does it matter?
3. What are the three apparitions' warnings, in order?
4. Who watches Lady Macbeth walk in her sleep?
5. How is each of the last two prophecies fulfilled?

Then say the play aloud in ten sentences, two per act. If you can, you can place any extract the exam prints.

check.solution: Macduff, the Thane of Fife, whose wife and children Macbeth had murdered, and who was untimely ripped from his mother and so not of woman born. The first apparition had warned Macbeth to beware him.

steps.title: Structure is a method: writing about it for AO2
steps.body:
Twelve of the thirty marks on the extract question are AO2, the writer's methods, and structure is one of them. The top level asks for fine-grained analysis of methods; structure done well is fine-grained.

**Name the choice.** Not *the murder is important* but *Shakespeare keeps the murder of Duncan off stage*, so the audience lives in Macbeth's imagination of it: the dagger before, the voice crying sleep no more after.

**Place the extract.** Every extract question gives a scene. Say where it sits in the rise and fall: Act 1 Scene 7 is the last moment Macbeth could have turned back.

**Use an echo.** An extract from Act 5 answers something from Act 1 or 2. Naming the pair is the whole-text move and a structural point at once.

**Tie it to the tragedy.** The shape is an argument about ambition: a rise that is over in two acts and a fall that takes three. When a structural point ends with what the shape says, it is doing the work the top level asks for.

boxes.title: The murder off stage
boxes.body: The audience lives in his imagination of it

boxes.title: Rise and fall
boxes.body: Crowned by Act 2; everything after is cost

boxes.title: Echoes
boxes.body: Heads, water, sleep: the end answers the start

visuals.alt: Four boxes on structural choices in Macbeth: the murder off stage, the rise and fall, the echoes, and the riddling prophecies, each with what it does

check.prompt: Which sentence would earn AO2 credit for analysing structure?
check.solution: The sentence about the murder off stage names a choice, says what it does to the audience, and ties it to Macbeth's mind. The others retell the plot in order, state a convention without an effect, or praise without analysis. Retelling is AO1 at best.

markScheme.description: By keeping the murder of Duncan off stage, Shakespeare makes the audience experience it as Macbeth does, through the dagger before and the voice crying sleep no more after

options: The murder of Duncan happens in Act 2, after Macbeth sees a dagger and before Macduff discovers the body, and then Macbeth is crowned king at Scone and the sons run away to England and Ireland
Shakespeare wrote Macbeth in five acts because all plays had five acts
By keeping the murder of Duncan off stage, Shakespeare makes the audience experience it as Macbeth does, through the dagger before and the voice crying sleep no more after
The structure of the play is very effective and keeps the audience interested

steps.title: The play in one page
steps.body:
A soldier praised and a prophecy half-fulfilled; a murder in Act 2 and a crown; a second murder that fails; a third that has no purpose; a wood that moves and a man not of woman born.

- **Act 1:** the witches, the battle, Cawdor, Malcolm named heir, Lady Macbeth's letter and her persuasion.
- **Act 2:** the dagger, the murder off stage, the grooms killed, the sons fled, Macbeth crowned.
- **Act 3:** Banquo killed and Fleance escaped; the ghost at the banquet; the turning point.
- **Act 4:** three apparitions; the murder of Macduff's family; Malcolm and Macduff in England.
- **Act 5:** the sleepwalking; the wood moves; Lady Macbeth dies; Macduff kills Macbeth; Malcolm is king.
- **Structure:** rise by Act 2, fall after; echoes of heads, water and sleep; prophecies true in word and false in hope.

The other Macbeth topics take the characters, the themes and the context; this one is the map they hang on.

visuals.alt: A summary table of the deaths act by act: the traitors of Act 1, Duncan and the grooms, Banquo, the Macduffs, and Lady Macbeth and Macbeth

check.prompt: In which act is Duncan murdered? Give the act number.
check.solution: Act 2. The murder happens off stage between the dagger speech and Macbeth's return with the bloody daggers, and the body is discovered by Macduff the next morning.

questions.prompt: What three titles do the witches greet Macbeth with in Act 1?
questions.solution: Glamis, which he already is; Cawdor, which he has just been given without knowing it; and king hereafter. The second comes true within minutes, and it is that fulfilled prophecy that makes the third feel possible.

markScheme.description: Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and king hereafter

options: Thane of Fife, Prince of Cumberland, and king of England, which is the title he later takes after the battle
Thane of Cawdor, Duke of Albany, and father of kings
General, Thane of Glamis, and Lord of the Isles
Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor, and king hereafter

questions.prompt: Who is named Prince of Cumberland, the heir to the throne, in Act 1?
questions.solution: Malcolm, Duncan's elder son. The naming turns the prophecy into a problem: Macbeth sees Malcolm as a step on which he must fall down, or else o'erleap, and asks the stars to hide their fires.

markScheme.description: Malcolm

questions.prompt: Where does Duncan stay on the night he is murdered?
questions.solution: At Inverness, Macbeth's castle, as a guest. The setting makes the murder a double betrayal: of a king by his subject and of a guest by his host, which Macbeth himself sets out in his soliloquy in Act 1 Scene 7.

markScheme.description: At Macbeth's castle at Inverness, as his guest

options: At Macbeth's castle at Inverness, as his guest
At his own palace at Forres, where the grooms who were meant to guard his chamber had been given drugged wine by Lady Macbeth
At Macduff's castle in Fife
In a tent on the battlefield

questions.prompt: How many kings are shown to Macbeth in the line of Banquo's descendants in Act 4? Give a number.
questions.solution: 8: eight kings, with Banquo's ghost following them, smiling and pointing at them as his. It is the promise of Act 1, that Banquo would get kings though he be none, shown as a procession, and it tells Macbeth that the murder of Banquo bought him nothing.

questions.prompt: Why is the murder of Macduff's wife and children the lowest point of Macbeth's fall?
questions.solution: Duncan was killed for a crown and Banquo to protect it. Macduff's family are killed after Macduff has already escaped to England, and they stand between Macbeth and nothing. Lady Macbeth has no part in it, and yet her sleepwalking line The Thane of Fife had a wife shows it haunting her.

markScheme.description: They threaten nothing: it is violence with no purpose but fear, done after Macduff has fled

options: Because Macduff's children were next in line to the throne after Malcolm and Donalbain, and so were a real threat to Macbeth's crown
They threaten nothing: it is violence with no purpose but fear, done after Macduff has fled
Because it happens in Act 5, just before his death
Because Lady Macbeth planned it

questions.prompt: Put these murders and deaths in the order the play presents them.
questions.solution: Duncan in Act 2, Banquo in Act 3, the Macduffs in Act 4, Lady Macbeth off stage in Act 5, and Macbeth at the end of Act 5. Each murder is further from any purpose than the one before.

markScheme.description: the five deaths in order

questions.prompt: What does Malcolm order his soldiers to carry, which makes the third prophecy come true?
questions.solution: Each soldier cuts a bough from Birnam Wood and carries it in front of him to hide the size of the army, so that the wood appears to move towards Dunsinane. A prophecy that seemed impossible comes true by a soldier's trick.

markScheme.description: boughs from Birnam Wood

questions.prompt: Which pair of lines is an echo between Act 2 and Act 5?
questions.solution: Lady Macbeth's Act 2 line about water and her Act 5 line about perfume are a pair: the blood that was easy to wash off is now a stain she cannot remove. Double, double is spoken by the witches, not Macbeth. The other pairs are not echoes of the same image.

markScheme.description: A little water clears us of this deed, and all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand

options: When shall we three meet again, and Lay on, Macduff
Is this a dagger which I see before me, and Double, double, toil and trouble, both spoken by Macbeth as he prepares for a murder
A little water clears us of this deed, and all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand
Fair is foul, and foul is fair, and Stars, hide your fires

questions.prompt: What happens at the banquet in Act 3?
questions.solution: The ghost of Banquo enters and sits in Macbeth's own seat, visible to him alone. His outbursts alarm the lords, and Lady Macbeth sends them away. It is the first time Macbeth's guilt shows in public, and it is the moment he decides to go back to the witches.

markScheme.description: Banquo's ghost sits in Macbeth's place, and only Macbeth can see it

options: Macbeth announces that Malcolm is his heir, and the lords, who have heard rumours about the death of Duncan, refuse to drink his health and leave
Lady Macbeth faints and the guests leave
Macduff accuses Macbeth of murder
Banquo's ghost sits in Macbeth's place, and only Macbeth can see it

questions.prompt: How does the play begin and end with a traitor and a head?
questions.solution: In Act 1 Macbeth kills Macdonwald and fixes his head on the battlements; the traitor Cawdor is executed. In Act 5 Macduff enters with the usurper's cursed head. The hero of the first scene has become the traitor of the last, and the structure makes the audience see it.

markScheme.description: It opens with the rebel Macdonwald's head fixed on the battlements and ends with Macduff holding up Macbeth's head

options: It opens with the rebel Macdonwald's head fixed on the battlements and ends with Macduff holding up Macbeth's head
Only the ending has a head; the opening has none
It opens with the head of Duncan on the castle gate at Inverness and ends with the head of Macbeth displayed by Malcolm at his crowning at Scone
It opens and ends with the witches holding a head

questions.prompt: Why might Shakespeare keep the murder of Duncan off stage?
questions.solution: The play shows other killings on stage, so the choice is deliberate. Kept off stage, the murder is felt through what Macbeth sees before it and hears after it, and the audience experiences it as he does: as imagination and guilt. That is a method with an effect, which is what AO2 asks for.

markScheme.description: So that the audience lives in Macbeth's mind: the dagger before, the voice crying sleep no more after, and the horror imagined

options: Because the murder is not important to the plot
So that the audience lives in Macbeth's mind: the dagger before, the voice crying sleep no more after, and the horror imagined
Because showing violence on stage was forbidden in 1606, and the Master of the Revels would have banned any play that showed a king being killed in front of the audience
Because the actor playing Duncan was needed for another part

questions.prompt: Macbeth says of Malcolm that he is a step on which he must fall down, or else what?
questions.solution: O'erleap: jump over. The same image of leaping returns in Act 1 Scene 7 as vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself, and the echo shows the ambition that began as a way over an obstacle becoming the thing that makes him fall.

markScheme.description: o'erleap

questions.prompt: The witches never tell Macbeth a lie. Why does that make the prophecies more dangerous, not less?
questions.solution: Banquo warns in Act 1 that the instruments of darkness tell us truths to win us to our harm. None of woman born and Birnam Wood are both true, and both are heard by Macbeth as guarantees. The witches never tell him to murder anyone; he chooses, and the truths lead him on.

markScheme.description: Their words are true but misleading, so Macbeth trusts them and hears safety where there is none

options: Because a true prophecy cannot be avoided, so Macbeth had no choice about any of the murders, which the play shows by making each one happen exactly as the witches said it would
Because the audience knows they are lying
Their words are true but misleading, so Macbeth trusts them and hears safety where there is none
Because Banquo believes them too

questions.prompt: Put these four moments of Macbeth's last day in the order Act 5 presents them.
questions.solution: Despair first, then his wife's death and the tomorrow speech, then the wood, then the last prophecy undone. Each piece of news removes a support, and Shakespeare orders them so that the final blow undoes the promise he trusted most.

markScheme.description: the four moments in order

items: Macbeth says he has lived long enough, and asks the doctor to cure his wife
He hears that the queen is dead and speaks of tomorrow
A messenger reports that Birnam Wood is moving
Macduff tells him he was untimely ripped from his mother's womb

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Shakespeare uses echoes between the beginning and the end of *Macbeth* to show the fall of Macbeth or Lady Macbeth. Name at least two echoes, say what each does, and connect them to the shape of the tragedy.
questions.solution: Shakespeare makes the end of *Macbeth* answer its beginning, so that the audience measures the fall in the play's own images. Lady Macbeth's confidence after the murder, “A little water clears us of this deed”, is answered in Act 5 by the woman who cannot stop washing, for whom “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand”: water that was to clear the deed has become a stain that no perfume can hide, and the distance between the lines is the distance she has fallen. The same pattern shapes Macbeth. In the first scene we hear how he “And fix’d his head upon our battlements”, the head of the traitor Macdonwald; in the last, Macduff enters with “Behold, where stands Th’ usurper’s cursed head”. The hero who displayed a traitor's head has become the traitor whose head is displayed, and the echo turns the rise and fall of a tragedy into a single visible picture. Even sleep returns: the voice that cried “Macbeth does murder sleep” after Duncan's death is answered by a queen who walks in her sleep. Because each echo pairs a moment of the rise with a moment of the fall, the structure itself makes the argument that the crime cannot be undone, the thing Lady Macbeth says in her sleep and did not believe when she was awake.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on where the turning point of *Macbeth* comes and why. Refer to at least two moments in the play and say what Shakespeare does with each.
questions.solution: The murder of Duncan is the top of Macbeth's rise, not the turn: it works, the sons flee, and he is crowned by the end of Act 2. The turn comes in Act 3, when his crimes stop working. He kills Banquo to stop the witches' promise that Banquo will get kings, but Banquo's last words, “Fly, good Fleance, fly”, save the son and keep the promise alive, so the second murder buys nothing. That night the ghost sits in his place at the banquet and he cries “Never shake Thy gory locks at me” in front of the lords of Scotland: the guilt that was private is now public. By the end of the scene he knows he cannot go back, “I am in blood Stepp’d in so far”, and he decides to return to the witches. Shakespeare places the turning point here so that the fall takes the second half of the play, and each crime after it is less useful and more terrible than the one before, until the murder of Macduff's family has no purpose at all.

questions.prompt: An exam extract is Act 5 Scene 1, the sleepwalking scene. Which whole-text move uses structure best?
questions.solution: The sleepwalking scene is built out of echoes: the blood, the washing, the knocking, the Thane of Fife. Pairing a line in the extract with the moment it echoes is a structural point and the whole-text move at once. Retelling what happens next is plot; the prose is worth a sentence, but only with what it does.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "The play is short and fast, which makes it exciting." What is the better account of the pace?
questions.solution: Shortness is a fact; the proportion is the method. Macbeth is crowned by the end of Act 2, and three of the five acts are given to what follows, so the play's weight falls on consequence rather than ambition achieved. The student has noticed the pace and stopped before its effect.

examTechnique.body:
**The extract is one scene; the question is the whole play.** Paper 1 Section A prints an extract from *Macbeth* and asks about it and about the play as a whole. Knowing the order of the play is what makes the second bullet possible.

**Place the extract.** A sentence on where it sits in the rise and fall is a structural point: Act 1 Scene 7 is the last chance to turn back; Act 5 Scene 1 is the fall measured.

**Use echoes for the whole-text move.** Water and perfume; murdered sleep and sleepwalking; the two heads. A pair of lines from two ends of the play does AO1 and AO2 at once.

**Retelling earns little.** Say what a structural choice does, not what happens next.
examinerErrors: Retelling the plot in order instead of saying what the structure does.
Getting the order wrong: Banquo is killed in Act 3, the Macduffs in Act 4.
Saying the witches lied, when their prophecies are true in word and misleading in meaning.
Saying Macbeth kills himself, or that Fleance kills him; Macduff does.
Staying in the extract and never placing it in the play as a whole.
Calling the murder of Duncan the turning point without saying why, when the crimes start to fail in Act 3.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats the play as built. It places the extract on the rise and fall, knows that the crown is won by Act 2 and that the crimes stop working in Act 3, and reads the murder off stage as a choice that puts the audience inside Macbeth's mind. For the whole-text move it pairs a line in the extract with the moment it echoes, so that one sentence measures a fall. Quotations are short, exact and placed in the right act, and each is followed by what it does.
